sections.body_en:
Preparing tefillin involves three components: (a) housings (batim), (b) straps, (c) passages, as will be explained further on in the chapter. In particular, the laws of preparing tefillin include many laws whose source is in the tradition of 'a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai'. They are: to make the tefillin square; to make the form of a 'shin' on the housing of the head tefillin; to sew the tefillin with sinews of a kosher animal; to make for the tefillin housings a ma'abarta through which the strap will pass; that the straps be black; to make in the head straps a knot like a 'dalet', and in the hand strap a knot like a 'yud' (Yerushalmi Megilla 1:9; Rambam, Tefillin 1:3).

The tefillin in all their parts must be made from kosher animals, including the parchment on which the passages are written, the leather from which the housings are prepared, the straps by which the tefillin are bound, and the sinews with which the tefillin are sewn. For it is said regarding the parchment on which the passages are written (Shemot 13:9): "And it shall be for a sign to you upon your hand and for a memorial between your eyes, so that the Torah of the Lord may be in your mouth", and the Sages interpreted (Shabbat 108a): "From what is permitted in your mouth", that is, from a species permitted to you for eating. And likewise the Sages said (Shabbat 28b) regarding all the other parts of the tefillin, "Only the hide of a kosher animal was made fit for the work of Heaven" (Shulḥan Arukh 32:12; 37; 44; 49; 33:3). Even the hide of nevelot and terefot of kosher species is valid for tefillin, for the main thing is that it be of a species that, if slaughtered properly, would be permitted to eat. But fish skin is invalid, because it has an impurity in it (Shabbat 108a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32:12).1

From the fact that the passages, the housings and the straps must be made from animal hide, one can learn that the supreme ideas penetrate and pierce down to the material sides of life, in order to reveal and awaken all the good in them, so that it too will join in revealing the word of God and His blessing in the world. But so that they can be properly revealed, they must be of species that are fit for Israel to eat.

notes_en.en: The explicit derivation from the Torah is that the parchment on which one writes must be of a kosher species (Shabbat 108a; Shulḥan Arukh 32:12); and it is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai that the housings, the sinews and the wrapping hairs be of a kosher species; and the Sages understood that the leather of the straps too must be of a kosher species, for only a kosher species was made fit for the work of Heaven (Shabbat 28b; Shulḥan Arukh 33:3; Mishna Berura 16).

sections.title_en: 2. Tanning the Leather and the Straps, and Making the Housings
sections.body_en:
The leather from which the housings and the straps are prepared must be tanned for the sake of the mitzva of tefillin (Shulḥan Arukh 32:37; 33:3). Tanning is done by placing the hide in lime or another substance, so that it draws out of it all the juices and acids, and in this way it can last for hundreds of years. Without tanning, the leather would rot within a short time.2

The tefillin housings may be prepared from the hide of a small animal, that is, sheep and goats, or from the hide of a large animal, that is, an ox, cow or calf. In the past almost all tefillin housings were produced from the hide of a small animal, whose hide is thin and easier to tan and prepare, but since it is not thick, it is hard to prepare housings from it with the utmost enhancement. In addition, over the years the housing, and especially its squareness, wears down and deteriorates. But they did not prepare tefillin from the hide of a large animal, because it is thick and no method had been found to tan it and prepare it in the form desired for tefillin. About a hundred and fifty years ago the way was found to prepare tefillin from the hide of a large animal, and since then it has been possible to prepare fine tefillin that last many years as if new. Today almost all tefillin are of the hide of a large animal.

One may make use of an electric machine to square the tefillin and to sand them, for although the pressure is applied by the force of the machine, and likewise the sander turns by electric power, it is the person who places the machine in the right place in order to press the square and to sand properly (Minḥat Shlomo 2:4; Divrei Yatziv 1:26). And some are stringent (Le-Horot Natan 11:1-3), but their reasoning is difficult, since in practice the person with his own hand uses the machine in order to square and sand the housings.

It is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai that the straps of the tefillin must be dyed black (below halakha 6). But as for the tefillin housings, in the view of many there is no mitzva to dye them black; rather, one may leave them in their natural colour or dye them any colour, and only for the sake of enhancing the mitzva are people accustomed to dye them black (the Rambam and the Rosh). And some say that it is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai to dye the tefillin housings black too (the Ri in Tosafot, Shabbat 28b, s.v. 'Tefillin'; the Baḥ; the Gra). In practice, it is a mitzva to dye the housings black, but this does not invalidate the mitzva (Shulḥan Arukh 32:40; Magen Avraham 33:6; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 32:79).

notes_en.en: According to the Rosh (Laws of Tefillin 3), one must tan the leather of the housings and the straps for its own sake, as in the words of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (Menaḥot 42b). And so wrote the Semag and the Terumah. However, according to the Rambam (Tefillin 3:15), only the straps require tanning for their own sake, but the leather of the housings does not need it, as in the view of the first Tanna there. The halakha follows the view of most Rishonim, except that when there is no choice it is better to fulfil the mitzva according to the Rambam (Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh 32:37), but without a blessing (the Baḥ; Eliya Rabba; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 67. And see Mishna Berura 171 and Bi'ur Halakha, s.v. 'Heikha').

sections.title_en: 3. The Housings of the Hand and Head Tefillin
sections.body_en:
It is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai that the tefillin housings have a titura and a ma'abarta. So the tefillin housings have three parts: (a) the 'bayit' (housing, also 'ketzitza'), in which the passages are placed. (b) the 'titura', which serves to close the housing from below. The titura is wider than the housing on all its sides, like the brim of a hat. In the wide area the tefillin are sewn with sinews in a double stitch, back and forth. There are three stitches on each side, so that on the four sides there are twelve stitches, corresponding to the tribes of Israel (Shulḥan Arukh 32:51; Mishna Berura 228). (c) the 'ma'abarta'. From the titura extends a ma'abarta, through which passes the strap by which the tefillin are bound to the arm and the head.

[Diagram: the parts of the hand tefillin.]

The tefillin housings have no set measure; therefore they may be made large or small. But they should not be too small, for then very small passages would have to be written for them, which are hard to write properly. And the housings should not be too large, for then the tefillin may extend beyond the place designated for putting on tefillin on the head and the arm (Shulḥan Arukh 32:41; Mishna Berura 189).3

For the hand tefillin the four passages are written on one parchment, which is placed inside the housing. By contrast, for the head tefillin the four passages are written on four parchments, and the square housing is divided into four narrow compartments, and one passage is placed in each compartment. This law was learned from a close reading of the verses (Menaḥot 34b). One can learn from this that in the head there is room for many different thoughts, but when one comes to action, there is a commitment to action and emotion that are consolidated as one; therefore all the passages in the hand tefillin are written on one parchment.

The tefillin housing must be made from one piece of leather. And even the housing of the head tefillin, which contains four compartments, must be of one piece of leather (Menaḥot 34b). Even when two pieces of leather are sewn or glued to each other, they have the law of one piece of leather. However, ideally people try to make the housing from one piece of leather without gluing or sewing. And some enhance the mitzva so that even the titura and the ma'abarta are of one piece of leather with the housings, without gluing. Today, when tefillin are made from the hide of a large animal, which is thick and large, it is easier to make them from one piece. Tefillin in which parts of other pieces of leather are glued are called 'simple tefillin' (tefillin peshutim).4

notes_en.en: The Rosh (Hilkhot Ketanot, abridged Laws of Tefillin) brought the words of the Shimusha Rabba, that ideally the tefillin housings must be the size of two fingers by two fingers – 3.8 cm (according to the Ḥazon Ish, 4.8 cm). And similarly wrote the Terumah (213) and the Semag (positive commandment 22). But the Rosh and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam wrote that people were not accustomed so. And so it was ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh 32:41. Today the prevalent custom is to take into account the words of the Shimusha Rabba, and the housings together with the titura are made two fingers (Eliya Rabba; Mishna Berura 32:189). Ḥabad Ḥasidim, following the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav (33:63), are particular that the housings alone be two fingers. And those who follow the Kabbala in putting on two pairs together, of Rashi and of Rabbeinu Tam, make the length of the housing with the ma'abarta two fingers, the measure of the housing itself being a little more than a finger (Va-Yeshev Ha-Yam 2:4). The Rosh further wrote there that one must take care that the housings with the titura not be smaller than a finger's width, and therefore there is room on the head for two tefillin housings and not three. Thus far. And there is concern that if they are smaller they will be invalid, since it will not be possible to write their passages properly (Olat Tamid 32:53; Mishna Berura 189). There were, however, those who were accustomed to make very small tefillin (Baḥ 32:27).

In the Gemara Menaḥot (34b): "He places them in four compartments in one piece of leather." Tosafot wrote (Menaḥot 32a, s.v. 'Dilma') that sewing two pieces of leather makes them one piece. And so wrote the Agudda (there) and the Ritva (Megilla 8b). The Or Zarua wrote (1:539) that gluing is like sewing. And so emerges from the Mishna (Kelim 18:8, as explained by the Rash, the Rambam, the Rosh and the Rav of Bertinoro). And the author of the Terumah wrote that ideally it is good to make them from literally one piece of leather, and his words were brought in the Beit Yosef (32:38); and so wrote Responsa Rema of Fano 38. And some Aḥaronim wrote that it is obligatory to make the tefillin from literally one piece of leather (the Baḥ; Keset Ha-Sofer 21:3; Yaskil Avdi 5:5). But almost all the poskim ruled that sewing or gluing makes the leather one, and so Israel were accustomed, except that ideally it is good to take into account the view of the stringent and to make the tefillin from one piece of leather (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 32:58; Responsa R. Azriel Hildesheimer 1; Mishna Berura 32:172; Mayim Ḥayim of Messas 2, 98:3; Yabi'a Omer 9, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1, and others). The Rishonim learned from Rashi and the Rambam that the titura and the ma'abarta too should be made from the continuation of the same leather from which the housing is made. And some hold that they may be made from separate pieces of leather even without gluing or sewing, and they wrote that so people were accustomed (Tosafot, Menaḥot 35a, s.v. 'Titura'; the Rosh and the Mordekhai). Today people are accustomed to be particular about this, and those who enhance the mitzva do not even make use of gluing (Mishna Berura 32:201).
If there are tears or holes in the leather of the tefillin housing or the titura and they are visible from outside, they are invalid (Menaḥot 35a; Shulḥan Arukh 33:1; Mishna Berura 6). If the holes in the housing of the head tefillin are in the leather between the four compartments, in a way that is not visible from outside: if they are in three compartments, they are invalid; if they are in one compartment, even several holes on both sides of that compartment, they are valid. If there are holes in two compartments and the compartments are adjacent to each other, even when the holes are not adjacent to each other, they are invalid. And if they are two compartments that are not adjacent, even though there are several holes in each of them, and in the inner one even on both its sides, they are valid (Shulḥan Arukh and Rema 33:1; Mishna Berura 9; Bi'ur Halakha, s.v. 'Rishon'). In any case there is no need to be lenient about this, for by gluing one can seal the hole and make it valid (see Mishna Berura 33:4). I wrote that the law of a hole is like the law of a tear, for this is the view of many (Lishkat Ha-Sofer 24:1; Sho'el U-Meshiv, third edition 1:298; and see Zikhron Eliyahu 12:5). However, some say that the whole invalidity is in a tear, which indicates the weakness of the leather, but a hole does not invalidate tefillin housings (Responsa Maharam Schick, Oraḥ Ḥayim 19-21; Beit She'arim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 27).

sections.title_en: 4. The Housing of the Head Tefillin
sections.body_en:
Each of the four compartments of the head tefillin must be separate from its fellow, with the walls of each of them surrounding it from the top of the tefillin down to the titura, and the groove between the compartments must be visible from outside along its whole length. After the fact, it is enough that the groove be noticeable at the top of the compartments, so that the four tops of the compartments are visible to all (Shulḥan Arukh 32:40).

One should not coat the four compartments with thick paint to the point that the grooves between the compartments are not noticeable at all. For even if grooves are made in the thick paint aligned with the real grooves, in the view of many they will be invalid. And if they are not aligned with the grooves, according to all views they will be invalid. When the tefillin are made from the hide of a large animal, which has thickness, people are accustomed to enhance the mitzva by cutting the leather a little around the grooves between the compartments, so that they will be noticeable along their whole length even after the tefillin are painted.

As we learned, the tefillin compartments must be separate from one another; the problem is that when they are separate they may move away from one another until the head housing is no longer square and becomes invalid (as explained in the next halakha). Therefore the scribes were accustomed to glue the compartments to each other a little, and as long as the gluing is over a minority of the surface between them, it does not invalidate (Bi'ur Halakha 32:40, s.v. 'Ḥaritz'). These tefillin are called 'mostly separated' (rov perudot). Today, when tefillin are made from the hide of a large animal, it can be made strong, so that even without glue its squareness will remain stable. These tefillin are called 'fully separated' (perudot male). Ideally people are accustomed to pass a sinew between the compartments at the height of the titura in order to separate the compartments (Shulḥan Arukh 32:51; Mishna Berura 230).5

notes_en.en:
Menaḥot (35a): "Abaye said: and the groove must reach the place of the stitching. Rav Dimi of Neharde'a said: since it is noticeable, it is not needed." Some say that this refers to the 'shin' on the tefillin, which ideally must reach the bottom of the housing, where the place of stitching is (the Ittur, Tefillin 58a; Ha-Manhig). And many hold that they are dealing with the grooves between the four compartments of the head tefillin, and ideally they must reach the place of the titura, as Abaye said, and after the fact it is enough that they be noticeable, as Rav Dimi said (Rashi; Rambam, Tefillin 3:11). In halakha one takes both explanations into account (the Rosh; Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh 32:40; 43).
Seemingly, according to what is explained in the previous note, gluing makes the pieces of leather count as one, and it turns out that gluing the tefillin compartments to each other invalidates them. And some ruled not to glue them (Ma'ase Rav, Tefillin 19; Siddur of the Admor Ha-Zaken; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 32:78). But people were accustomed to glue them, because without this the compartments moved away from each other, the squareness deteriorated and the tefillin became invalid (Ḥatam Sofer; Lishkat Ha-Sofer 21:3). And some explained that only gluing intended to unite the parts of the leather is considered uniting gluing, which is not so of gluing intended to keep the separate compartments from moving apart (Yeshu'ot Yaakov 32:24; Ḥatan Sofer 24:1; Bar Leva'i, Oraḥ Ḥayim 3). And some added and explained that since in practice four compartments remain there, as long as the grooves are noticeable from outside the gluing has done no harm (Ḥelkat Yo'av 1, first edition, Yoreh De'ah 34; Da'at Torah 32:40). In order to satisfy the stringent, people were accustomed to spread the glue on the lower part close to the titura, in a way that only a minority of the surface of the compartments is glued and the grooves are noticeable (see Bi'ur Halakha 32:40, s.v. 'Ḥaritz'). As said above, in housings of the hide of a large animal they can be made fully separated without gluing. This enhancement is called 'fully separated' (perudot male). Some are meticulous to leave a gap visible to the eye between the compartments, and call this enhancement 'grooved tefillin' (tefillin ḥarutzot). But many hold that there is no reason for this meticulousness, which was not prevalent in Israel, and in addition, it may also cause the squareness to deteriorate.
In tefillin of small-animal hide there were those who were accustomed to cover the compartments with leather and make grooves in it, and some say that if the grooves were made aligned with the real grooves they are valid (Maharam Mintz 61; Har Tzvi 1:34). And some invalidate them (Parashat Mordekhai 2; Bigdei Kehuna 1).
In the Gemara (34b): "He puts a thread or a cord between each one." Some explain that this law is for exceptional cases (the Semak, Orḥot Ḥayim). And some hold that the intention is to put a thread between the compartments, in order to distinguish between compartment and compartment (Rambam 3:11; Semag 22). After the fact, the lack of this thread does not invalidate (Taz 32:38; Mishna Berura 230). Today some enhance the mitzva by passing the sinew between the compartments at the height of the titura after the tefillin have been completed, in a way that it is noticeable from outside, and call this enhancement 'aligned tefillin' (tefillin mekhuvanot). However, by the letter of the law there is no need for this. Ideally people are accustomed to make the tefillin compartments equal to one another, for the beauty of the tefillin (Darkhei Moshe 32:16, in the name of the Rokeaḥ).

sections.body_en:
It is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai that the tefillin must be square, that is, that their length be equal to their width, and the diagonals too must be equal, so that the housing will be a square and not a rhombus. Both the titura and the stitches in the titura must be square too. So that the ma'abarta will not be considered part of the titura and turn it into a rectangle, the edge of the titura is cut in such a way that the distinction between it and the ma'abarta is noticeable.

[Diagram: the squareness of the housings.]

One can say as a reason for the mitzva that the square housing hints at the Holy of Holies, which is also square, for the tefillin are meant to draw the holiness of the Temple to each and every one of Israel, as it is said (Shemot 25:8): "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" – among them, within each and every one of Israel (see Zohar I 129a). The shape of the circle is closer to the shapes found in nature, and Israel, who keep the Torah and the mitzvot, draw straight lines into the world in order to guide and repair it, and through them the blessing of God is drawn into the world. And when the lines form a square, their blessing becomes fixed and stable. Therefore the Holy of Holies and the tefillin are square (see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 30:2).

This squareness need not be absolutely precise, for the Torah was not given to the ministering angels but to human beings, and whatever looks square to the eye is considered square. In practice, up to a deviation of 2% it certainly looks square to the eye. Likewise, the tefillin are not invalidated when the points of the corners wear down over time and become slightly round (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 32:77). If the tefillin were square at first and over time their squareness deteriorated, if this is plainly noticeable, so that any person sees it at first glance, they are invalid and one may no longer recite a blessing over them (Shulḥan Arukh 32:39).6

notes_en.en:
The Sages said (Menaḥot 35a) that the diagonals too must be squared, so that it will be a square and not a rhombus. Rashi explained that the intention is the measure the Sages gave (Sukka 8a) for the diagonal: "Every amma in a square is an amma and two fifths in the diagonal." That is, the diagonal must be 1.4 times the side of the square. And so it was ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh 32:39. But it is known that this measure is not precise; rather it is about 1.414, and consequently, in calculating a square according to a diagonal of 1.4, there will be a difference of a little more than 2% between the length and the width. So in the view of the Sages a difference of two percent is still considered entirely square. Indeed, an ordinary person does not notice a change of two percent (and so wrote Igrot Moshe, Yoreh De'ah 3:120; Yabi'a Omer 9, Oraḥ Ḥayim 6:3-5; Halikhot Shlomo 4:25). However, the more the tools of work and measurement are refined, the more it is right to be precise in the squareness (Eretz Tzvi 1:12). If tefillin were made properly square and over time their squareness was damaged, only if this is noticeable to most people at first glance should they be invalidated; for otherwise one would have to invalidate most tefillin, which until a hundred and fifty years ago were made mainly from the hide of a small animal and undoubtedly did not remain precisely square as at first (Ikarei Ha-Dat 2:12; Imrei Yosher 2:64). Likewise, the tefillin are not invalidated when the points of the corners wear down over time and become slightly round, for this is their way, and the squareness in general remains whole. And so wrote the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (32:77), for "the Torah was not given to the ministering angels, and damage to the corners is unavoidable"; and indeed there are craftsmen who make strong housings, but they "take much money for their housings, which not every person can afford", and even the points of the expensive housings "deteriorate a little" over time (and so wrote Gilyon Alfas, Ḥullin 8a; Yabi'a Omer 9, Oraḥ Ḥayim 6:7).
The squareness must be made by the leather and not by a thick coating glued onto it (Noda Bi-Yehuda, Oraḥ Ḥayim, first edition 1; Mishna Berura 32:178). Included in damage to the squareness is when in the head tefillin the compartments separate from one another until it is noticeable that they are not square.

sections.body_en:
Binding the tefillin to the arm and the head is done by means of the tefillin straps. As we learned (halakhot 1-2), the straps must be made from the hide of a kosher animal, and they must be tanned for the sake of the sanctity of tefillin.

The width of the straps must be at least the length of a barleycorn (Shulḥan Arukh 27:11), which is about one centimetre. In practice people enhance the mitzva by making the straps about a centimetre and a half wide. Even when the strap has become creased at the place where it is tightened and is now less than a centimetre wide, since if it were straightened out it would be a centimetre wide, it is valid.

The length of the hand strap is enough to bind the tefillin with it on the muscle of the arm, and from there it continues to the middle finger, around which it is wound three times. And people are accustomed to lengthen the strap so as to wind it around the arm seven times (Shulḥan Arukh 27:8), and to wind it on the palm and the fingers in a form that hints at the letters 'shin' and 'yud' (Tashbetz 3:118). There are different customs about this, and all are valid, and it is right for each person to continue the custom of his forefathers.

The length of the head straps is enough to tighten the tefillin on the head and for them to hang down in front of him, the right one to the navel and the left one to the heart. And people are accustomed to enhance the mitzva by lengthening the right strap to the place of circumcision and the left one to the navel (Tur and Shulḥan Arukh 27:11; Mishna Berura 27:41; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 52; above 3:5). After the fact, if the head straps were cut and at least two tefaḥim of them remain, he should put them on with a blessing. And if less, he should put them on without a blessing (Mishna Berura 27:44).

It is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai that the straps must be dyed black (Menaḥot 35a). The dyeing must be on the outer side of the strap (Shulḥan Arukh 27:11; 33:3). Some are stringent, following the Rambam, to dye the inner side black as well, and the custom in the past was to leave the inner side in its natural colour.7

Preparing the straps and dyeing them must be done by a Jew for the sake of the sanctity of tefillin (Rema 33:4; Mishna Berura 22-23). If a little of the black colour has faded, as sometimes happens at the place where the straps are tightened and at the 'yud' and 'dalet' knots, the black colour should be renewed for the sake of the sanctity of tefillin. And this can be done with any black marker whose colour is fast.8

notes_en.en: From the Gemara (Menaḥot 35a) we learned that the inner side of the straps may be of any colour except red. And so it was ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (33:3). However, according to the Rambam (Tefillin 3:14), the intention of the Gemara is that the inner side of the straps must be the colour of the housing. Thus far. According to this, since the housings are dyed black, the inner side of the straps must be dyed black too. And some hold that this is right and fitting according to halakha and Kabbala (Ḥesed La-Alafim 33:4; see Ben Ish Ḥai, Ḥayei Sara 4). But most poskim hold like the Shulḥan Arukh, that one need not dye the inner side of the straps, and so is the custom (Beit Yosef; Darkhei Moshe; Mishna Berura 21, and many others). And since many were accustomed so, some hold that those who are stringent in this appear to cast aspersions on the earlier generations. But in our days, when the price of dye has fallen, it is convenient for the dyers to dye the straps on both sides, since the dyeing is done by immersion. That being so, dyeing both sides casts no aspersions on the earlier generations, and at the same time it satisfies all the views.

Some say that the black colour must be entirely black like a raven (Tikkun Tefillin; Keset Ha-Sofer 23:2), and some say that it is enough that it be considered black in people's eyes (Da'at Kedoshim 33:1), including even if there are small spots on the straps that are not black (Halikhot Shlomo 4:28). If the colour has peeled, some say that if most remains black it is valid (Responsa Maharshag 1:7; Or Le-Tziyon 2, 44:39). But it is accepted to rule that all the straps must be black (Mishna Berura 33:19). One may renew the colour with a black fountain pen or a black marker, and even according to those who hold that the dye must be from something that is not forbidden to eat (Tikkun Tefillin; Yeshu'ot Yaakov 32:27), there is no concern today, since the dyes are not produced from animals.
According to the Shulḥan Arukh (33:4), it is good that a Jew dye the straps for their own sake, which implies that after the fact a gentile may do it. But according to the Radbaz (1:153) and the Rema, a Jew must do it, and it is good that he say 'for the sake of the sanctity of tefillin'. And so is the custom.

sections.title_en: 7. The Letters of the Name on the Tefillin and the Straps
sections.body_en:
It is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai to make the form of a 'shin' in the leather of the head tefillin housing on both its sides: the 'shin' on the right of the one wearing them with three heads, and the 'shin' on his left with four heads – three corresponding to the Patriarchs and four corresponding to the Matriarchs. The lower edge of the 'shin' must reach the titura (Menaḥot 35a; Shulḥan Arukh 32:42-43). In the view of many, by the letter of the law it is enough to make the 'shin' in the simplest way, but people are accustomed to enhance the mitzva and make it in the form of a 'shin' in STaM script (Mishna Berura 191). Some hold that the 'shin' should not be made by stamping with a mould, because in this way the 'shin' is not written but comes about by itself through pressing what surrounds it (Rabbeinu Yona, the Rashba). And some hold that there is no flaw in this, and on the contrary, it is good to make it with a mould so that it will be beautiful (Or Zarua 563; Rema of Fano 38; Mishna Berura 193). Today people enhance the mitzva by making the 'shin' with a mould, and afterwards they moisten the leather and undo the 'shin', and again raise the 'shin' by handwork with tweezers; and this is then done easily, for the leather 'remembers' the form of the 'shin' that was stamped into it. In order to complete the 'shin' in its beauty and elegance, they go back and finish making it with a mould.9

The Sages further said (Menaḥot 35b) that it is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai to make the letter 'dalet' in the straps of the head tefillin, and the letter 'yud' in the strap of the hand tefillin. Together they form the Name 'Sha-ddai'. It is good to prepare the letters in their order: first to finish preparing the head tefillin housing with the letter 'shin', then to tie the 'dalet' in the head straps, and finally the 'yud' in the strap of the hand tefillin (Rema 32:52).10
There are two customs in making the 'dalet' knot in the head straps: some make a square knot, and the 'dalet' is formed by the straps extending from the knot, and some make the knot itself in the form of a 'dalet'. Both customs are valid, and it is right for each person to continue the custom of his forefathers. The 'yud' knot made in the hand strap is close to the tefillin housing (see above 3:6).

notes_en.en: Three explanations were given for the reason of the right and left 'shin' (Barukh She-Amar, brought in Eliya Rabba 32:65-66). Their idea is that the right 'shin' corresponds to the action of man, and the left 'shin' corresponds to receiving the Divine revelation and the special character of Israel, which is the receptive side in man: (a) The right 'shin' corresponds to human writing, and the left corresponds to the engraved Divine writing on the Tablets of the Covenant, the four lines being those that surround the three lines of the 'shin'. (b) Three heads correspond to the weekdays on which the Torah is read, which express the active side, and four heads correspond to the four days on which the Torah is not read, which express the receptive side. (c) Three correspond to the Patriarchs, who are the active side, and four correspond to the Matriarchs, who are the special receptive side (see Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-Bayit U-Virkhato 10:2).

Menaḥot (35b): "The knot of the tefillin is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai." And in Shabbat (62a), three statements of Abaye: "The shin of the tefillin is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai… the dalet of the tefillin is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai… the yud of the tefillin is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai." And so wrote Rashi (Menaḥot 35b, s.v. 'Kesher'). However, Tosafot (Shabbat 62a, s.v. 'Shin') read in the Gemara that only the 'shin' on the housing of the head tefillin is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai. And what they said in Menaḥot, "the knot of the tefillin is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai", refers to the very fact that one must make a knot in order to tighten the tefillin, but the form of the letters in the straps is a custom (the Ittur, Tefillin 59b).

sections.body_en:
The Torah commanded that there be four passages in the tefillin: 'Kadesh' (Shemot 13:1-10), 'Ve-haya ki yevi'akha' (there 11-16), 'Shema' (Devarim 6:4-9), 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' (there 11:13-21), and these are the passages in which the mitzva was stated to put them in the hand tefillin and in the head tefillin.

The scribe must write the four passages in two copies. For the head tefillin he writes them on four parchments, in order to place each passage in its own compartment, and for the hand tefillin he writes all four passages on one parchment, in order to place it in the housing of the hand tefillin (above halakha 3).

The laws of writing the passages will be explained in the laws of STaM (chapter 10), and the laws that concern writing the passages of the tefillin will be explained below.

Inserting the passages into the tefillin: the passages are rolled from their end to their beginning. It is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai that the rolled passages must be wrapped in hair. People were accustomed to use the hair of a calf, in order to atone for the sin of the golden calf. Ideally the passages are also covered with parchment; therefore the rolled passages are wrapped in calf hair, covered with parchment, and again wrapped in calf hair, and so they are inserted into the housings. (The order of the passages will be explained below in halakha 10.)

The passages are stood with their top facing upwards and the beginning of their opening facing the one standing opposite the wearer, so that they are in a form fit to be read. People are accustomed to pull out a little of the calf hair wrapped around the passage of 'Ve-haya im shamo'a', so that it will be visible from outside (Shulḥan Arukh 32:44-46; Mishna Berura 211-212).

sections.title_en: 9. Open and Closed Passages in the Tefillin
sections.body_en:
The passages of the tefillin must be written as they are in the Torah: the first three open (petuḥot) and the fourth closed (setuma) (an explanation of closed and open passages below 10:16). In addition, each of the passages must be written in a separate column. For the first three passages there is no problem: one begins to write them at the beginning of the line, as is accepted for beginning open passages. Before the first passage one need not leave a space of nine letters, since it begins the order of the passages, but at the end of the first and second passages one leaves a space of nine letters for the space that the following open passage must have. But the fourth passage, 'Ve-haya im shamo'a', cannot be written as a closed passage according to the views of both the Rambam and the Rosh, for since it must be written in a separate column, there is no form in which it will be closed according to both views (as explained in the note). Therefore it is made closed according to the view of the Rambam. That is, the third passage, the passage of 'Shema', is finished at the end of the line of the previous column, and the passage of 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' is begun in the middle of the line, after a space the size of nine letters. And although according to the view of the Rosh it is thereby considered an open passage, the halakha is that when it is impossible to satisfy both views, one acts according to the view of the Rambam (Shulḥan Arukh 32:36; below 10:16).11 In addition, some say that after the fact, if he made the last passage open, the tefillin are valid, because although it is itself a closed passage, since in the Torah there are many open passages between the passage of 'Shema' and the passage of 'Ve-haya im shamo'a', there may be the space of an open passage between them (the Ittur; Rema there; Mishna Berura 158); so it turns out that in their view, the tefillin are valid even according to the Rosh.

And in the view of the Taz (32:26), one can make the passage of 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' closed according to all the views, that is, he leaves at the end of the passage of 'Shema' less than the measure of nine letters, and begins the passage of 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' in the next column after less than nine letters; and since there is no space of nine letters in one place there, according to all views it is considered a closed passage. And so many of those of Ashkenazi origin were accustomed. But on the other hand, some hold that since there is no continuous space of nine letters there, it is not considered a new passage but a continuation of the previous passage, and the tefillin are invalid. In practice, it is right for each person to continue the custom of his forefathers.12

notes_en.en: According to the Rosh, in order to make a closed passage there one must leave a space of a whole line and begin the fourth passage at the beginning of the following line, except that in this way it will be considered open according to the Rambam. And if one finishes the third passage in the middle of the line, leaving a space of more than the measure of nine letters to the end of the line, and begins the fourth passage at the beginning of the line, it will be considered open both according to the Rosh and according to the Rambam. See below 10:16 for an explanation of these laws.

Preceding the Taz were Responsa Maharam of Padua 77, the Maharshal 37 and the Rema of Fano 106. But it is usual to call this view by the name of the Taz. Most of the Ashkenazi Aḥaronim supported this view, among them: the Gra, the Peri Megadim (Mishbetzot Zahav 26) and the Keset Ha-Sofer (20:7). And the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan wrote (32:63): "And most of the great of Israel agreed to this, and so it is done in most of the dispersions of Israel" – meaning in Europe. And the Mishna Berura (32:164) leaned to this.
But on the other hand, some say that those who follow the Taz do not fulfil their obligation, for his proposal is not good according to the Rambam and the Shulḥan Arukh. And in Yeḥaveh Da'at (4:3) he ruled that those of Sephardi origin should not put them on and should not recite the blessing over them. And so wrote Responsa Ish Matzli'aḥ (1, Yoreh De'ah 44). And the Or Le-Tziyon (2, 3:7) agreed, and added that if he has no others he should put them on without a blessing. But on the other hand, from the Ḥida (Ḥayim She'al 1:59) it is implied that after the fact he has fulfilled his obligation. And it was likewise reported in the name of Rav Ezra Attia (Sefer Ha-Zikaron Knesset Ezra, p. 89, item 20) that on a temporary basis (thirty days) those of Sephardi origin may fulfil the mitzva according to the Taz with a blessing.
And so it appears in practice, both according to the principle 'we do not multiply disputes' – that it is not right to widen disputes, and whenever it is possible to explain them in a narrowing way, this is what should be done, and here too it is fitting to rule according to those who hold that in a pressing situation those of Sephardi origin may rely on the custom of those of Ashkenazi origin. And as the Rema wrote (Yoreh De'ah 275:2), based on Mahari Mintz 8, regarding a Torah scroll, that although the halakha follows the Rambam, "if a Torah scroll is found that is not written according to his words, it should not be invalidated, for there are great authorities who have other reasonings in this" (see below 8:6, note 7).
In addition, according to the rules of halakha too, on the basis of combining doubts, it is fitting to rule that one of Sephardi origin may, when necessary, borrow tefillin from one of Ashkenazi origin and recite the blessing over them: (a) It may be that these tefillin were written according to the Rambam's view, for there are Ashkenazim who act so, and usually the owner of the tefillin does not know about it. (b) Although those of Sephardi origin were accustomed to rule not according to the Taz and those with him, one may add the view of the Taz to the doubt, that perhaps the halakha follows his view and the spaces combine. (c) It may be that at the beginning of 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' there is the space of a passage according to some of the views, and if so, the passage is closed according to the Rambam's view. That is, there may be there the measure of 9 small letters, which is the space sufficient to make a closed passage according to the Beit Yosef in the Rambam's view. And according to the reading of Rabbeinu Tam and the Rosh in tractate Soferim (1:15-16), even a space of three letters is enough to make it a closed passage, and according to the Ḥida (Ḥayim She'al 1:59) this is in practice the view of the Rambam. And the following took this view into account: the Rosh (Mezuza 5), the Semag (positive commandments 23), the Semak 154, the Tur (Yoreh De'ah 288), the Mishna Berura (32:110). And some hold that even a space of two letters is enough to make it closed, which is the view of Siddur Kadmonim (brought in Tosafot, Menaḥot 32a, s.v. 'Ve-ha-idna'). (d) It may be that at the end of the passage of 'Shema' there is the space of a passage according to some of the views (as explained in the previous doubt), and if so the passage is considered open, and some hold that if he made 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' open it is valid (the Ittur, Orḥot Ḥayim, Rema 32:36; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 58-59, in the Rambam's view). (e) Even if the spaces that were left do not form the space of a passage, some hold that a closed passage in tefillin does not require a space, or requires a small space, and they are: the Perisha (288:14) in the view of the Rosh and the Tur, and so wrote the Derisha (275:2), the Riaz (in the Shiltei Ha-Gibborim on the Rif, Mezuza 5) and the Eshkol (Mezuza, p. 71b). And so emerges from the Ra'avya (Megilla, end of 548) and the Or Zarua (Megilla 373), that closed passages of tefillin and mezuzot require a smaller space.

sections.body_en:
In the period of the Rishonim a great dispute arose about the order of the passages of the head tefillin. According to Rashi and the Rambam, the order of the passages is as their order in the Torah: on the right side the passage of 'Kadesh', after it 'Ve-haya ki yevi'akha', after it 'Shema', and last, on the left, 'Ve-haya im shamo'a'. But according to Rabbeinu Tam the third passage is 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' and the fourth is 'Shema'. Right and left are determined according to one standing opposite the one wearing the tefillin, so that the passage on his right side is the right one. And they likewise disagreed about the hand tefillin: according to Rashi and the Rambam the third passage is 'Shema' and the fourth 'Ve-haya im shamo'a', and according to Rabbeinu Tam the third is 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' and the fourth 'Shema'. However, even according to Rabbeinu Tam's view they must be written in the order in which they appear in the Torah: first 'Shema' and after it 'Ve-haya im shamo'a'. Since the order of the passages is indispensable, it turns out that according to Rashi's view the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam are invalid, and likewise the reverse.

Although the dispute is called by the names of Rashi and his grandson Rabbeinu Tam, its roots are ancient, from the days of the Geonim. The Geonim of the Land of Israel and the author of the 'Shimusha Rabba' followed the view of Rashi, and Rav Sa'adya Gaon and Rabbeinu Ḥananel followed the view of Rabbeinu Tam.

Apparently, until the days of Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam this question had not yet arisen in its full sharpness, and consequently the halakha was not decided either; rather, there were important communities that followed Rashi and there were those that followed Rabbeinu Tam. But following the raising of the question, in the generations after them the custom accepted in Israel was according to the view of Rashi and the Rambam, as was the practice in the beit midrash of the Ramban, without taking into account the view of Rabbeinu Tam.

And there were Rishonim (the Terumah, the Rosh) who ruled that ideally a God-fearing person should put on two pairs of tefillin because of the doubt. And they used to put them on together, for the Sages said that there is room on the head and the arm for two pairs of tefillin, and so they prayed and recited the Shema with both pairs. And they made a condition in their minds that their intention was to fulfil the mitzva according to the view that is correct in halakha. But when the tefillin are of large housings, like most housings in our days, there is no room on the arm and the head for two pairs, and one who wants to put on the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam puts them on after the prayer.13

notes_en.en:
Menaḥot (34b): "The Rabbis taught: What is their order? 'Kadesh li' and 'Ve-haya ki yevi'akha' on the right, 'Shema' and 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' on the left… Rav Ḥananel said in the name of Rav: if he switched its passages, they are invalid." According to Rashi (there) the order is continuous, as the order in the Torah, so that the third passage is 'Shema' and the fourth 'Ve-haya im shamo'a'. And so emerges from the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael (Masekhta de-Pisḥa 18). And according to Rabbeinu Tam, if the order were continuous, the order of the passages would have been stated continuously; from the fact that they said two on the right and two on the left, we learned that the two on the right begin from the right side inwards, and the two on the left begin from the left side inwards, so that the third passage is 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' and the fourth 'Shema'. And so it is brought in the Tikkunei Zohar (Introduction 9a) in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud. Although the dispute between the customs is ancient, as explained above, it is accepted to call the view of 'passages in their order' 'the view of Rashi', and the view of 'the havayot in the middle' (that is, the passages of 'Ve-haya' and 'Ve-haya' in the middle) 'the view of Rabbeinu Tam'.
The Rambam too wrote like Rashi (Tefillin 3:5), and he explained in a responsum (289) that when he was in the West (Spain and north-west Africa) he followed Rabbeinu Tam, as the Rif had practised, and when he came to Egypt he saw that all the people of the Land of Israel and its surroundings followed Rashi, and he received testimony that so the Geonim of the Land of Israel and Rav Hai Gaon had practised, and therefore he changed his custom to the view of Rashi. And so wrote the Ittur. On the other hand, it is brought in Tosafot (Menaḥot 34b, s.v. 'Ve-ha-kore') that Rav Hai Gaon, Rabbi Yosef Tov Elem and Rabbeinu Ḥananel held the view of Rabbeinu Tam. And many wrote their words and added that this is also the view of Rav Sherira Gaon (the Terumah, the Rosh, and others). And Rabbi Yehuda of Barcelona wrote that he had not heard of anyone who followed Rashi's view, and this matches the testimony of the Rambam that in Spain he followed Rabbeinu Tam.
Apparently, following Rabbeinu Tam's objection to Rashi, as brought in Tosafot, the dispute came to the top of the agenda; there were those who continued their custom, according to Rashi or Rabbeinu Tam, and many inclined to follow Rashi. And some of the greatest Rishonim (the Terumah, the Rosh, the Tur and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam) wrote that a God-fearing person should satisfy both of them and make two pairs of tefillin in order to escape the doubt. And they used to put them on together and intend with the blessing that it apply to the tefillin that were written properly. And so wrote the Semag (positive commandments 22) and the Hagahot Maimoniyot, except that they agreed that the prevalent custom in their days was according to Rashi. But in the beit midrash of the Ramban they followed Rashi and were not concerned about Rabbeinu Tam's view. As the Rashba wrote (Meyuḥasot 234), that so the Ramban and Rabbeinu Yona practised, and so wrote Responsa Rashba (1:639) and the Ḥinukh 421. In parallel, in Ashkenaz, so wrote the Mordekhai (Tefillin 969). And the Maharil (137) wrote that people follow Rashi, and only one who is "established and renowned for piety" puts on both pairs. Apparently, following the position of the great authorities of Spain, the Ramban and his students, who decided according to Rashi, the halakha was accepted according to Rashi, and the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan wrote (34:3) that even those who take Rabbeinu Tam into account recite the blessing over those of Rashi, "as if a heavenly voice had gone forth that this is the halakha". And so it was ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (34:1-3).
As we learned above, the order of the passages is from right to left, that is, according to how it appears to one standing opposite the wearer. But some hold that the right is according to the wearer, so that there are two further views: In Responsa Rema of Fano he wrote that the view of the 'Shimusha Rabba' is like Rashi but reversed. And so wrote the book Matzat Shimurim (although from the plain wording of the Rishonim it is implied that the 'Shimusha Rabba' is like Rashi in every respect). According to the Ra'avad in the name of Rav Hai Gaon (on the Rambam, Tefillin 3:5), the order is like Rabbeinu Tam but reversed, and he explained that since the tefillin are closed, there is no reason to go by the right of one standing opposite the wearer, but by the wearer, since the tefillin are for him; therefore one goes by the right of the wearer. According to the Rambam (Responsa 289) and the Semak 153, in the hand tefillin everyone agrees to Rashi's view. And according to most poskim, according to Rabbeinu Tam's view the order must be changed in the hand tefillin too.

sections.body_en:
A great question arises from the dispute: how is it possible that in a matter whose tradition continued from generation to generation, a fundamental dispute arose, to the point that according to each view one does not fulfil the obligation according to the other view? After all, tefillin are made by traditions that are a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai, so how is it possible that someone should suddenly arise and change the custom, until two customs came into being?

One can explain that this is indeed the calamity of the exile: in the wake of the upheavals of the exile and the persecutions, the traditions became confused, and so a mistaken custom came into being, and the Rishonim disagreed about which was the correct custom and which the mistaken one.

And in the view of the Kabbalists, as the holy Ari explained, both views have value, for each view expresses an intention and a unification of its own; if so, ideally there is room to put on both pairs of tefillin, in order to allude to both intentions. According to this it is understood that both traditions have ancient roots, as became clear when tefillin from the days of the Tanna'im were found, some according to Rashi's view and some according to Rabbeinu Tam's view.

Similarly, some say that according to halakha the order of the passages is not indispensable, and the whole discussion is how it is more fitting to fulfil the mitzva, and consequently it is understandable that there were different views about it. And even if we hold that according to the Sages the order of the passages is indispensable, by Torah law it is not indispensable, and therefore they were not so meticulous in transmitting this tradition.14

notes_en.en:
The first explanation, that the upheavals of the exile caused the doubt and the dispute, is understandable, and it appears to be agreed upon by many, and it is mentioned in many discussions (see Rambam, Shofar 3:2). Similarly, the Eshel Avraham (Butchach, Oraḥ Ḥayim, end of 493) wrote that the dispute arose in the wake of times when the mitzva of putting on tefillin was weak in Israel because of the persecutions, until only exceptional individuals put on tefillin (as explained above 3, note 2).
However, the Ari (Sha'ar Ha-Kavanot, Derushei Tefillin, Derush 6) explained that both views have value: the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam issue from 'moḥin de-Abba' and those of Rashi from 'moḥin de-Imma', and in this world the halakha follows Rashi and in the World to Come it will follow Rabbeinu Tam. The basis of his words is in the Tikkunei Zohar Ḥadash (14a). Following his words, they explained that since both views have value, it is understandable that there were two customs, only that they disagreed about which custom was the main one for halakha, and there were exceptional individuals who were accustomed to put on two pairs. And so wrote the Emunat Ḥakhamim 30 and Mitpaḥat Sefarim 104. And tefillin from the period of the Tanna'im were indeed found, some according to Rashi and some according to Rabbeinu Tam, which shows that both customs existed in Israel as valid customs, like what Rav Hai Gaon explained regarding the customs of the teru'a (Appendices to 'Torah Shelema' 1, by Rav M. M. Kasher; the notes of Rav Margaliyot on Responsa Min Ha-Shamayim, pp. 45-46; Rav Goren, Torat Ha-Mo'adim, p. 534). And so it is brought in the Piskei Tosafot (Menaḥot 34b, item 92) that "in Neharde'a and in Jerusalem they found two pairs – one according to Rashi and one according to Rabbeinu Tam". And the Ben Ish Ḥai (Vayera 21) even went so far as to write that from the days of Moshe Rabbeinu they used to put on two pairs.
According to this it is reasonable that by the essential law one can fulfil the obligation with either of the pairs. And so wrote Responsa Besamim Rosh 24, that there are Geonim who explained that the order of the passages is not indispensable; in their view, after Abaye (Menaḥot 34b) explained that "if he switched its passages they are invalid" refers to switching between the outer and the inner ones, but if he switched an inner one with an inner one or an outer one with an outer one it is valid, Rava disagreed with him and held "there is no difference", that all changes of the passages are valid (in contrast to the accepted explanation, that according to Rava all changes invalidate). And he wrote that even for those who disagree with this, "there is no doubt that this invalidity of the order of the passages is not a Torah law". And this was brought by Rav Yitzḥak Tayeb (Vavei Ha-Amudim on the Yere'im, Amud Ha-Yir'a 16, end of item 1), the Maharsham (Da'at Torah 34:2) and Rav Kasher in the Appendices to 'Torah Shelema' (siman 1). And so wrote the Da'at Kedoshim (34:2) on his own reasoning, in the language of doubt, and he wrote that this offers a defence of the general custom of putting on only the tefillin of Rashi.

sections.body_en:
In the Shulḥan Arukh it is ruled that the custom is according to Rashi, and a God-fearing person should put on both pairs; but it stressed that "only one who is established and renowned for piety should do so". And it wrote that one who puts on both pairs should recite the blessing over those of Rashi. And one who puts them on together should be careful to intend that he is fulfilling the mitzva with those that are valid according to the truth, for if he does not intend so he transgresses the prohibition of 'do not add' (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 34:1-3; and see there the Mishna Berura and Bi'ur Halakha).

However, the Kabbalists disagreed with this on two points. The first: in their view one should intend to fulfil the mitzva with both pairs, for there is a virtue in both of them. The second: in their view it is fitting for every person of Israel to put on two pairs, and not only God-fearing people who are established and renowned for piety (Maḥazik Berakha, Oraḥ Ḥayim 34:2).

By contrast, in the view of the Gra, even a God-fearing person renowned for piety need not put on the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam, because the halakha has been decided according to Rashi and the Rambam. And if we were to take into account all the different views in the laws of tefillin, we would need to put on sixty-four pairs every day. Rather, the way to fulfil the mitzvot of the Torah is according to the halakha that has been ruled, and according to the custom of Israel, which is Torah, and therefore it is enough to put on one pair only. And so is the prevalent custom.

In practice, it is fitting for every person to act according to the custom of his forefathers. And if he has a distinguished rav – as his rav will guide him.15

notes_en.en:
For those who hold that a God-fearing person should put on two pairs because of the doubt, one must be careful to intend that one wishes to fulfil the obligation with what is valid according to halakha, while the other is like mere straps; for otherwise, in the view of many, he transgresses the prohibition of 'do not add' by Torah law (the Baḥ), or by rabbinic law (the Taz and the Maḥatzit Ha-Shekel), as explained in the Mishna Berura (34:7), the Sha'ar Ha-Tziyun 8, and Yabi'a Omer (1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 3). However, according to the Ari and those with him, since both are correct, one should fulfil the mitzva with both pairs. And the Ben Ish Ḥai (Vayera 22) explained that the blessing is not recited over those of Rabbeinu Tam because of their exalted level, for we do not have the power to draw down the light that flows from their level (and see Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 17:11, on matters of halakha and Kabbala).
In Tosefet Ma'aseh Rav 18 it is brought that Rabbi Ḥayim of Volozhin asked the Gra: "Granted that the master does not put on the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam, so as not to neglect tefillin for even one moment, and those of Rashi are the main ones. But I, who in any case neglect tefillin for several hours, what does it matter if I put them on for some hours of the day and fulfil the obligation of tefillin according to all the views? And he answered him: If you want to fulfil all the views, you will need to put on twenty-four pairs." And in Si'aḥ Eliyahu the reading is sixty-four pairs. He further asked: "But it is found in the Zohar about the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam that they are of the World to Come. And he answered him that the plain meaning of the Zohar is not so, and one who pursues the World to Come may put them on. And from the day he heard the words of the living God from his holy mouth, he stopped putting them on." And this is the calculation brought there regarding sixty-four pairs: (a) Rashi. (b) Rabbeinu Tam. (c) The Ra'avad, who is like Rabbeinu Tam but reversed. (d) The Rema of Fano in the view of the 'Shimusha Rabba', which is like Rashi but reversed. That makes four pairs. "And Tosafot wrote in Menaḥot… Rabbeinu Tam used to say that they are placed lying down and not standing… (see Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh 32:45); if so, eight pairs are needed, to resolve this doubt too. There is a further doubt regarding the parchment, whether on the thick side, on the flesh side or on the hair side, as the Kesef Mishneh wrote from a responsum of the sages of Lunel to our Rabbi about this doubt… (see below 10:4, note 3); if so, that makes sixteen pairs. There is a further doubt regarding open and closed passages – the form of the Rambam and the form of the Rosh (above halakha 9); that makes thirty-two pairs. Further: ink from the soot of wood and not from gall water, which Rabbeinu Tam invalidates and the Rambam and the Rosh validate (below 10, note 5). That makes sixty-four pairs. Rather, the halakha decides according to Rashi…".
In practice, many of those who follow the halakha, both of Ashkenazi origin and of Sephardi origin, follow the Shulḥan Arukh (34:2) and put on the tefillin of Rashi only, and only God-fearing people established in piety also put on those of Rabbeinu Tam, making the condition that they are fulfilling the mitzva only with the tefillin that are correct according to the truth. And so wrote the Levush (34:2), the Magen Avraham 3, the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 4, the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 4, Yabi'a Omer (1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 3), and many others. And so was the practice in Syria, Iraq and Egypt, that only "the pious and men of deeds" put on both (Pada et Avraham 2, p. 292). And likewise in Tunis, only the rabbis put on two pairs (Alei Hadas, Tefillin 32). And some follow the Gra, and even those renowned for piety put on those of Rashi only. This is the custom of almost all the rabbis who pray in Nusaḥ Ashkenaz. And likewise in Yemen, the rabbis were not accustomed to put on the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam (Etz Ḥayim, Laws of Tefillin, 'Ve-seder ha-parshiyot'; Pe'ulat Tzaddik 3:216). In Morocco too, there was almost no one who put on the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam, rabbis included (Shemesh U-Magen 3, Oraḥ Ḥayim 58:4).
And those who follow the Kabbala put on both pairs; some put them on together, and most put on those of Rashi for the main part of the prayer and those of Rabbeinu Tam at the end of the prayer. And even those who put them on together do not make a condition, because according to the Ari both pairs are needed, and both are true. So wrote the Matzat Shimurim (Laws of Tefillin); Responsa Ḥayim She'al (1:1), Yafeh La-Lev (Shiyarei Yafeh La-Lev 34:1), and others. And the Or Le-Tziyon (2, 3:8) wrote that he should make the condition that "if the truth is as the Kabbala – I am putting on both of them for the sake of the mitzva of tefillin, and if the truth is as the plain meaning – I intend to fulfil the obligation with those that are according to the halakha, and the rest are like mere straps". Among those who follow the Kabbala are most Ḥasidim (from Eastern Europe), who follow this practice from the age of bar mitzva.

sections.title_en: 13. Buying Tefillin and Mezuzot from a God-Fearing Scribe
sections.body_en:
One must buy tefillin and mezuzot from a God-fearing person, on the reliability of whose testimony one can rely that the tefillin or mezuzot he sells are valid. But one who buys them from a person who is not known takes the risk that they are invalid, and no meticulous examination will be able to reveal it. For example, if the scribe did not intend before writing them that he was writing them for the sake of the mitzva of tefillin or for the sake of the mitzva of mezuza, or forgot to intend to write the Names for the sake of the sanctity of the Name – the tefillin are invalid, and this is not discernible in an examination. Likewise there are cases where an error occurred that invalidates the tefillin or the mezuza and there is no way to correct it because of 'not in their order' (below 10:15), and if the scribe is not honest, he may correct the error in a forbidden way, so as not to lose the passages on which he laboured for many hours, and the proofreaders have no way of knowing this. And sometimes the scribe does not know the halakha properly, for example he wrote a letter by way of 'ḥok tokhot' (below 10:13), and does not know that he has thereby invalidated the tefillin or the mezuza.

Therefore, one should buy tefillin and mezuzot from a God-fearing scribe who is expert in the laws of STaM, or alternatively from a God-fearing dealer who markets passages by scribes known to him as God-fearing and expert in the laws of STaM. Since outward appearance cannot testify to the reliability of the seller, one who does not personally know a God-fearing scribe or dealer who is expert in the halakha would do well to turn to a rav he knows, so that he may advise him where to buy tefillin and mezuzot.

Fear of Heaven is tested in honesty and reliability between a person and his fellow, and in readiness to forgo money so long as one does not stumble into the prohibition of theft or falsehood. In addition, it is an enhancement of the mitzva to buy tefillin from a righteous scribe, who is meticulous in the mitzvot between a person and God and in the mitzvot between a person and his fellow, sets times for Torah and prays with a minyan, pays taxes according to the law and fulfils the mitzva of settling the Land. And if he is also among the soldiers who risked their lives in defence of the people and the Land, his merit is especially great.

If a person bought passages that were written by a God-fearing scribe and underwent a proper examination, and after some years he opened them and it turned out that they have an invalidity, in the view of many, since he did what was incumbent upon him in checking the tefillin he bought, he is considered as one who fulfilled his mitzva. This is similar to what the Sages said (Kiddushin 66b) regarding a kohen who served in the Temple and it turned out that he is the son of a divorcee, who is disqualified from the priesthood: although from then on every offering he brings is invalid, the offerings he brought until then on behalf of Israelites are valid, and they need not bring them again (Da'at Kedoshim 39:9).16

notes_en.en: Some argued against this that one can bring a contrary proof from the Gemara there, that a blemished kohen who brought offerings without knowing that he was blemished – his offerings are invalid (Yabi'a Omer 7, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5). However, one can answer that one cannot learn from the law of a blemished kohen, because the blemish is a discernible thing, and there is negligence in not knowing that he is blemished. Rather, the law of the tefillin is similar to a kohen who through no fault of his own did not know that he was the son of a divorcee, since this is not discernible. And so wrote the Peri Ha-Sadeh (3:117), Sha'arim Metzuyanim Ba-Halakha (10:3) and the Tzitz Eliezer (22:1), and similarly wrote the Rav Pe'alim (Oraḥ Ḥayim 4:2). Mishaps of this kind occur because, very rarely, the proofreader became confused and thought he had proofread the passages when in fact he had not proofread them, or perhaps out of tiredness he did not find the error, or when inserting the passages they erred and inserted other passages. In practice, when tefillin are bought from a God-fearing dealer, these mishaps are rare.

sections.title_en: 14. Enhancing the Mitzva and How Much It Is Right to Pay for It
sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to enhance the mitzvot, as it is said (Shemot 15:2): "This is my God and I will glorify Him" – "Beautify yourself before Him in mitzvot" (Shabbat 133b). And likewise we find that God accepted the offering of Hevel, who brought an offering of the firstlings of his flock and of their fat, while He did not accept the offering of Kayin, who was stingy and brought of the plain fruit of the ground (Bereshit 4:3-5; Rambam, Issurei Mizbe'aḥ 7:11).

The Sages said that the mitzva of enhancement is to add up to a third of the price of the mitzva (Bava Kamma 9a). For example, if valid tefillin of the hide of a large animal, which will last a long time, cost about 2,000 shekels, then the mitzva of enhancement is to add up to a third and buy more enhanced tefillin for 2,666 shekels. And some are stringent and hold that the third is 'from outside', that is, that the addition should be a third of the total price, and then the enhancement is to buy them for 3,000 shekels. And if he wants to enhance the mitzva and add more than a third, in order to buy more enhanced tefillin, the Holy One, blessed be He, will pay his reward. This is on condition that the additional enhancement does not come at the expense of other mitzvot that take precedence in importance, and all the more so not at the expense of paying his debts and providing for the basic needs of his household.

The mitzva of enhancement applies to an ordinary person, but one whose situation is straitened has no mitzva to add a third (Yam Shel Shlomo, Magen Avraham, Mishna Berura 656:6). On the other hand, one who has been granted wealth should enhance and add more than a third. And especially one who is accustomed to enhance in buying clothes and furniture at a price much higher than the price of ordinary clothes and furniture, for whom it is a mitzva to add and enhance in mitzvot at least as much as he adds for weekday needs.

Included in enhancement is satisfying the views of those who are stringent even though they have not been ruled as halakha, and seeing to it that the tefillin and the straps are beautiful, and even enhancing by having a handsome bag in which the tefillin are kept, and replacing it when it wears out.

Some tefillin makers pride themselves on long lists of meticulous details and enhancements, but it is hard to be impressed by them, because most of the details they list are present in most tefillin, and some of them concern remote concerns or laws that have no basis in the poskim. Therefore, it is right for one who is not expert in the details of the enhancements to buy from a scribe or dealer who is known as reliable and God-fearing, as explained in the previous halakha.17

notes_en.en:
The laws of enhancing a mitzva were explained in the Expansions to Peninei Halakha, Sukkot 4:14, and the dispute was brought whether the mitzva of enhancement is from the Torah or rabbinic, and it appears that certainly there is also a Torah mitzva to enhance the mitzvot, only the definition of the enhancement as a third is from the words of the Sages.
In the Gemara (Bava Kamma 9b): "Rav Ashi asked: a third from inside or a third from outside? Let it stand." For example, if the price is 2,000, then a third from inside is 666, and from outside 1,000. The Rosh was lenient, and so ruled the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 656:1) and most of the Aḥaronim. However, many Rishonim were stringent, among them: Rabbeinu Ḥananel, the Ran, the Ra'avan and the Riaz. And so wrote the Yam Shel Shlomo (Bava Kamma 1:25), the Baḥ (656:1) and the Eliya Rabba 3.
The Sedei Ḥemed (Kelalim, Ma'arekhet Zayin 12) wrote that it emerges from the words of Rabbeinu Tam (Tosafot, Menaḥot 32b, s.v. 'Ha') that there is no mitzva to enhance the beauty of what is hidden, and therefore one need not score lines for the passages of tefillin. And so wrote the Petaḥ Ha-Devir. However, the Mordekhai, the Rema (32:4) and others wrote that the mitzva is to beautify the tefillin outside and inside.
Included in enhancement is taking into account stringent views that were not ruled as obligatory in halakha (Peri Megadim, Mishbetzot Zahav 656:1; Avnei Nezer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 484; Bi'ur Halakha 656:1, s.v. 'Im kana'). And likewise buying a handsome bag for the tefillin, just as people seek out a handsome case for jewellery (Sefer Ḥasidim 129).
Seemingly, it would be possible to make do with adding a third to the price of tefillin of the hide of a small animal, whose price is about 1,000. But since they do not last many years, it is more worthwhile to buy tefillin of a large animal, which last several times as many years. Therefore it is more correct to calculate according to the price of tefillin of the hide of a large animal, as I wrote above. A further drawback of such cheap tefillin is that, since the seller's profit is very small, there is a concern that in order to remain profitable he will rely on the most lenient opinions in questions concerning the validity of the housings or the passages, and will take passages that were written hastily or by unskilled scribes. However, in practice, one who wants tefillin of a small animal may take as his base the low price that a reliable dealer offers him for valid tefillin.

sections.body_en:
Tefillin that have a presumption of validity, that is, that were properly checked when they were made, never need to be checked again, and as long as they have not been damaged they are presumed valid and are put on with a blessing. This is on condition that the tefillin are put on regularly. But if they fell into water, or were not put on for a prolonged period, one must hasten to check them, in order to make sure that no invalidity has occurred in one of the letters (Shulḥan Arukh 39:10). One who is accustomed to keep his tefillin in the car, where they are sometimes exposed to very high heat, should have them checked twice in seven years.18

It must be noted with regret that sometimes, when tefillin are given to be checked, even though the tefillin are in good condition, the checker looks for flaws in them and finds them, in order to cause the owner of the tefillin to buy new passages from him and to pay him for renewing the tefillin. He is indeed careful in his language and stresses that it is not clear whether the flaws he found invalidate, but he explains that in order to escape doubt it is better to replace the passages and renew the housings. Sometimes this is a checker from a particular circle who views other circles with a jaundiced eye, and therefore his heart inclines him to find problems in the passages and tefillin of scribes and makers from other circles. But had the owner of the tefillin turned to a checker from the circle of the scribe or the maker, he would have found that the tefillin are valid and fine.

The reason that flaws can be found even in valid passages is that the writing is done by hand, and naturally the letters are not uniform, and there are differences between scribes; therefore, when one wants to, one can often find some letter that was written slightly differently and cast a certain doubt on it. In addition, over the years the tendency to enhance and be stringent has grown, and the more printing has spread in the world, the more the form of the letter has become fixed at higher standards, so that what was once considered enhanced is now considered merely valid, and what was once considered valid is now considered valid with problems. Even passages that were written about forty years ago by God-fearing scribes, and were then considered valid without question, there will be proofreaders today who will cast doubt on their validity. Within this framework it is easy too for a checker who does not wish the passages well to find flaws in them, even though they were written by the finest scribes. However, the Sages warned against casting aspersions on the earlier generations, and those who cast doubt on the form of the letters of God-fearing scribes of previous generations are sinning. And the Sages already said (Avot 5:19) that the disciples of Avraham Avinu have 'a good eye'. The law of tefillin that have worn out and their burial – below 14:10.

notes_en.en: In the view of most poskim, and so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (39:10), there is no need to check tefillin that are put on regularly. However, in the view of many Aḥaronim, it is right ideally to check them twice in seven years, because they may have been spoiled by sweat (Mishna Berura 39:26). And the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (39:6) wrote that it is obligatory to check them, because it is known that sometimes over the years the ink flakes off the parchment. And some wrote that it is a measure of piety to check the tefillin every year in the month of Elul (Mateh Efrayim 581:10; Kitzur Shulḥan Arukh 128:3). On the other hand, Tosafot wrote (Eruvin 97a, s.v. 'Ha-loke'aḥ') that checking tefillin also involves a degradation of the tefillin. And so wrote the Mekor Ḥayim (by the Ḥavot Ya'ir, 39:10). Therefore one should not check them unnecessarily. In practice, today, when tefillin are made of the hide of a large animal, they are protected much more than in the past, and the concern that they have become invalid has fallen away. And so the custom is not to check them. And so wrote Halikhot Shlomo (4:36), that in our time one need not take into account the stringency of the Aḥaronim to check tefillin twice in seven years. (And so it wrote regarding a mezuza when it has been sealed in plastic, below 6:10.) And we have likewise heard from veteran proofreaders that even after tefillin have been in very great heat and have even become wet, it is very rare that an invalidity is found in them. Therefore, if they were not kept properly, for example one is accustomed to leave them in the car in very high heat, it is right to check them twice in seven years. And if, as a result of the heat or the wetness, the stitches have come open, one must check them immediately.
